title: Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities
content:
2.2 Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities

Overview: WP5 as the structural home of dissemination, exploitation, and communication

The fellowship's dissemination, exploitation, and communication programme is contained within WP5 — Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management — which runs from month 1 through month 24 under the lead of Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, with Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest as a contributing participant. WP5 produces two deliverables that together govern and document the full span of the programme: the Data management plan (D5-01, due month 6), which establishes the governance framework for open science, FAIR data stewardship, and the licensing architecture that underpins all subsequent release activities; and the Dissemination and communication activity report (D5-02, due month 24), which records the complete evidence base of dissemination, communication, and exploitation activities carried out across the fellowship's lifetime. These two deliverables create a temporally anchored accountability structure: D5-01 establishes forward-looking commitments early in the fellowship when methodology design is still being finalised, ensuring that open-science principles are designed in rather than retrofitted; D5-02 closes the loop at the project's end, providing a verifiable audit trail against which the commitments of D5-01 can be assessed.

WP5 operates continuously from month 1 rather than being deferred to the final phase of the fellowship. This is methodologically significant: dissemination and communication activities that are deferred to the final months of a 24-month fellowship cannot be adapted in response to the scientific results as they emerge. By initiating WP5 from month 1 alongside the research work packages, the programme ensures that dissemination planning evolves in real time with the scientific content of WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state), WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), and WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration), and that interim results — for example, methodological advances from WP1 that can be presented at a conference in the second year before the full validation in WP3 is complete — are exploited as they become available rather than held for a single end-of-project release.

Target groups and the rationale for differentiated communication

The fellowship's output profile — a probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state diagnosis methodology (OUT-1: Probabilistic multi-sensor field-state diagnosis method), an uncertainty-aware AquaCrop-based decision engine (OUT-2: Uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine), a field-validated dataset and calibration evidence (OUT-3: Field-validation dataset and uncertainty-calibration evidence), a standalone end-to-end demonstrator (OUT-4: Standalone research demonstrator (web MVP)), and a set of open-access publications and scientific data releases (OUT-5: Peer-reviewed publications and open science outputs) — is relevant to three substantively distinct target groups, each of which requires a differentiated communication register and a different dissemination channel.

Target Group 1: The international scientific community in geoinformatics, remote sensing, probabilistic machine learning, and crop-water science. This group is the primary addressee of the project's scientific claims: the probabilistic multi-sensor fusion-to-diagnosis framework, the end-to-end honest uncertainty chain, the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration methodology, and the field-validation evidence base are all contributions to knowledge that are evaluated and adopted within the peer-reviewed scientific literature. This group is geographically international, institutionally diverse, and accessed primarily through open-access publications, preprint repositories, and the major international scientific conferences in remote sensing and geoinformatics. The project's novelty claim — the end-to-end coupling of learned multimodal fusion, explicit probabilistic crop-water-state outputs, and water-use-efficiency-oriented irrigation decision support in an area the reviewed literature identifies as underdeveloped — defines this group's specific interest in the project's outputs and justifies the emphasis on rigorous, peer-reviewed dissemination as the primary scientific-impact mechanism (IMP-1: Scientific advance in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation).

Target Group 2: Hungarian tomato and horticulture farmers connected to AgroVIR, together with precision-agriculture extension advisers and agronomic practitioners who use Earth-observation-based crop management tools. This is the applied-sector audience for whom the project's core decision objective — water-use efficiency under uncertainty (RQ6) — is operationally relevant. Unlike the scientific community, this group is not reached through peer-reviewed publications or international conference presentations. Communication to this group requires the research demonstrator (OUT-4: Standalone research demonstrator (web MVP), TRL 3-4, RQ10) as the primary medium: a working end-to-end system that presents irrigation recommendations alongside their uncertainty in a form that is intelligible to practitioners, together with the field validation evidence from WP3 that gives the recommendations biological credibility. AgroVIR — the confirmed associated partner providing farmer access and field-validation feedback at Hungarian tomato farm sites — is the operative communication channel for this group. AgroVIR's role in WP3 (providing the field sites for the validation protocol and the farming-sector feedback loop) makes the practitioner-engagement communication activities structurally integrated into the project's scientific validation programme, not a separate public-engagement afterthought. This integration is a key strength of the fellowship's impact architecture: the communication to Group 2 and the scientific validation work of WP3 are co-produced at the same field sites, by the same partnership, using the same demonstrator, with the result that each reinforces the credibility of the other.

Target Group 3: ELTE's geoinformatics and remote-sensing academic community — Faculty of Informatics staff, postgraduate students, and junior researchers in multi-sensor remote sensing and agri-environmental modelling. This group is the host institution's internal scientific community, whose exposure to the project's evolving probabilistic fusion and uncertainty-calibration methods constitutes the direct academic beneficiary of the two-way knowledge transfer governed by WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge). Communication to this group takes the form of structured knowledge-exchange events — seminars, lab meetings, and teaching contributions within the ELTE geoinformatics environment — that integrate current project results into the host's academic practice as they emerge. This communication is governed jointly by WP4 (where the two-way knowledge exchange is formalised in the Career Development Plan (D4-01, due month 3)) and WP5 (where the events are recorded in D5-02, due month 24).

Dissemination plan: scientific activities and open-science commitments

Open-access peer-reviewed publication is the primary mechanism for scientific dissemination and the means through which the project's contributions to the state of the art in probabilistic multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation are permanently embedded in the scientific literature. The project's scientific outputs span three distinct methodological contributions — the probabilistic multi-sensor field-state diagnosis method (OUT-1, anchored in WP1 and reported in the Multi-sensor data harmonisation and diagnostic model report (D1-01, due month 14)), the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine (OUT-2, anchored in WP2 and reported in the Decision engine and research demonstrator report (D2-01, due month 20)), and the field-validation dataset and uncertainty-calibration evidence (OUT-3, anchored in WP3 and reported in the Field validation and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, due month 24)) — each of which constitutes a distinct publishable contribution in peer-reviewed journals at the intersection of remote sensing, precision agriculture, and probabilistic modelling. All peer-reviewed publications arising from the project will be made immediately open access upon acceptance, in compliance with MSCA open access mandates and Plan S where applicable; preprints will be deposited in discipline-relevant repositories. The default is immediate open availability; no embargo periods beyond those required by specific journal publishing agreements will be applied. This commitment is established formally in D5-01 (Data management plan, due month 6) and its fulfilment documented in D5-02 (Dissemination and communication activity report, due month 24).

The FAIR data and model release is the second scientific dissemination mechanism. The calibrated Bayesian hierarchical fusion models, multi-sensor EO datasets (Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, secured PlanetScope imagery, ERA5 meteorological reanalysis), and AquaCrop uncertainty parameter posteriors produced in WP1, WP2, and WP3 will be archived under FAIR principles — findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable — with persistent DOIs as specified in the project Data management plan (D5-01, due month 6). The release of these artefacts alongside the open-access publications is not merely a compliance action; it is an active dissemination mechanism that enables the geoinformatics and precision-agriculture research community to build on the validated probabilistic fusion-to-decision methodology independently of the fellowship's continuation, without the need to repeat the fellowship's foundational derivation. This directly increases ERA R&I capacity (EI-05: Increased R&I capacity, output, and knowledge transfer among European research organisations) by providing validated open artefacts that survive the fellowship duration and can support follow-on research targeting other crops and regions. The open release is governed by D5-01 (which specifies the datasets, the licensing terms, and the persistent-DOI infrastructure) and evidenced in D5-02. Software artefacts — including the probabilistic fusion pipeline and the standalone research demonstrator — will be released under a permissive open-source licence (MIT or Apache 2.0).

International conference presentation is the third scientific dissemination mechanism. The project's results — particularly the calibration evidence (RQ5: 90% prediction-interval coverage) and the Route B patch-covariation test (RQ9) — are presented to the peer audience in the remote sensing, geoinformatics, and precision-agriculture research community at relevant international venues. These presentations serve a different function from open-access publication: they enable real-time scientific dialogue, receive peer challenge on methodology and interpretation, and integrate the project's results into the evolving scientific conversation in a timeframe that allows course correction where necessary. Conference activities are planned to occur at the rate of at least one presentation per project year and are recorded in D5-02 (Dissemination and communication activity report, due month 24). The fellowship's confirmed international mobility — Dr. Rositsa Cholakova moving from Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute, Bulgarian Agricultural Academy, Plovdiv, Bulgaria to Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest — positions the fellow to access the Central and Eastern European geoinformatics and remote-sensing research community as well as the broader European and international conference circuit, broadening the project's scientific reach.

Communication activities: the applied-sector and public-engagement dimension

The research demonstrator showcase constitutes the primary communication mechanism for Target Group 2. The Standalone research demonstrator (web MVP) (OUT-4, TRL 3-4, RQ10) — an end-to-end system that exercises the full observation-to-decision pipeline, presenting irrigation recommendations with their honest uncertainty bounds — is demonstrated to AgroVIR and to Hungarian tomato farmers connected to AgroVIR in at least one documented farmer-facing session completed by month 20, as recorded in the Decision engine and research demonstrator report (D2-01, due month 20). This demonstration is not an academic presentation but a translation exercise: the project's probabilistic output must be communicated in a register that is meaningful to practitioners for whom water-use efficiency (RQ6) is a farm-management concern rather than a scientific hypothesis. The demonstrator's role as a communication artefact is inseparable from its role as a scientific artefact: the same system that proves the scientific claim (an end-to-end pipeline from multi-sensor observation to uncertainty-aware irrigation decision) communicates the applied relevance of that claim to the practitioners who could eventually benefit from its operational deployment. This dual function — scientific demonstrator and applied communication vehicle — makes the demonstrator development in WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) one of the most impact-efficient activities in the fellowship: a single artefact generates both IMP-1 (scientific advance) and IMP-2 (Economic and societal impact: water-use efficiency and farm resilience) and directly addresses EI-03 (Broadened public engagement with research and innovation) through practitioner engagement.

Knowledge-exchange events at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest constitute the communication mechanism for Target Group 3. At least one documented knowledge-exchange event per project year — in the form of a seminar, lab meeting, or teaching contribution in the ELTE geoinformatics and remote-sensing environment — integrates current project results (probabilistic fusion diagnostics, AquaCrop uncertainty calibration findings, field-validation evidence) into the host's academic practice. These events serve the call's expected outcome EO-08 (Regular feedback of research results into teaching and education at participating organisations) and the corresponding impact EI-06 (Enhanced integration of current research results into higher education and teaching at host organisations). They are planned jointly through WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge) — which formalises the two-way knowledge exchange in the Career Development Plan (D4-01, due month 3) — and recorded in D5-02 (Dissemination and communication activity report, due month 24). The result is that the project's research results flow into ELTE's academic community not as a retrospective summary at project end but as an evolving contribution integrated into the host's seminar and teaching calendar throughout the fellowship's 24-month duration. Dr. András Jung's position as Deputy Head of the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics and his dual habilitations in Computer Science and Crop Sciences ensure that the knowledge-exchange events reach both the computational geoinformatics and the applied crop-science dimensions of the host's academic community, maximising the breadth of integration.

Exploitation plan: maximising long-term use of project outputs

The project's exploitation strategy is calibrated to its TRL 3-4 scope. At a research-prototype TRL target (RQ10), the primary exploitation route is not commercial licensing or immediate operational deployment; it is the open release of validated research artefacts that enable the geoinformatics and precision-agriculture research community to build on the fellowship's foundational work without duplication of effort, and the use of the demonstrator as a documented proof-of-concept for follow-on funding bids targeting higher TRL deployment. The exploitation plan accordingly comprises three complementary activities.

Open methodology and codebase release for community reuse. The probabilistic multi-sensor fusion-to-irrigation-decision framework — comprising the calibrated diagnostic pipeline (OUT-1), the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine (OUT-2), the open validation data and protocol (OUT-3), and the research demonstrator (OUT-4) — is released as a documented, reusable open-source codebase under a permissive open-source licence. The release is governed by D5-01 (Data management plan, due month 6), which establishes the licensing terms and persistent-DOI infrastructure, and timed to accompany the open-access publications by month 24. The expected result of this exploitation activity is a reusable, documented probabilistic multi-sensor fusion-to-irrigation-decision framework available to the geoinformatics and precision-agriculture R&I community, enabling follow-on research targeting other crops and regions without repeating the fellowship's foundational derivation. This directly supports EI-05 (Increased R&I capacity, output, and knowledge transfer among European research organisations) by providing validated open artefacts that outlast the fellowship duration and strengthen the European Research Area's scientific base in agri-environmental Earth observation.

Research demonstrator as proof-of-concept for follow-on funding. The Standalone research demonstrator (web MVP) (OUT-4, D2-01, due month 20) and its documented field-validation evidence (D3-01, due month 24) — including the 90% prediction-interval coverage target (RQ5) and the Route B patch-covariation test (RQ9) — constitute a publicly available proof-of-concept that the fellow and AgroVIR can reference in follow-on funding bids targeting operational TRL 5-6 deployment. The demonstrator documents that the probabilistic fusion-to-decision pipeline has been assembled and validated at a level sufficient to serve as the foundation for a higher-TRL development programme. This exploitation route connects IMP-2 (Economic and societal impact: water-use efficiency and farm resilience) to a longer-term pathway toward operational uptake, without asserting commercial impact that would be disproportionate to a 24-month research fellowship. The demonstrator is documented in D2-01 by month 20 and is available as a follow-on proposal reference from month 24 onward, with AgroVIR's agronomic feedback documented as part of WP3 validation by month 24.

Knowledge transfer embedding in the host research group. Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest retains the probabilistic multi-sensor fusion expertise and cross-disciplinary training infrastructure embedded through the structured two-way knowledge transfer in WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge). This exploitation activity ensures that the project's scientific contribution does not end when the fellowship ends: the host's geoinformatics and remote-sensing group acquires durable embedded expertise in probabilistic crop-water-state modelling and non-destructive stress phenotyping through the fellowship's 24-month programme, equipping it to supervise follow-on PhDs and postdoctoral researchers in agri-environmental Earth observation and to compete for subsequent agri-EO grants leveraging the validated methodology. This activity is formalised in the Career Development Plan (D4-01, due month 3), recorded in WP4's training activity log updated at mid-project, and sustained through the knowledge-exchange events documented in D5-02 (due month 24). The expected result directly supports EI-05 (Increased R&I capacity, output, and knowledge transfer among European research organisations) and EO-07 (Stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations; better transfer of knowledge).

Intellectual property strategy and protection measures

The project produces academic research outputs at TRL 3-4. No patent applications are anticipated. The primary exploitation route is open publication and open-source software release, consistent with MSCA open science requirements and the project's commitment to FAIR data stewardship as governed by D5-01 (Data management plan, due month 6). This IPR posture is the appropriate and proportionate strategy for a single-researcher postdoctoral fellowship producing a research prototype: the scientific value of the outputs is maximised by making them openly available and reusable, not by restricting access through patent protection.

AgroVIR's agronomic validation datasets — collected at Hungarian tomato farm sites as part of the WP3 field-validation programme — will be handled under data-sharing terms agreed between Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest and AgroVIR and documented in the Data management plan (D5-01, due month 6). This arrangement ensures that AgroVIR's proprietary agronomic data is protected under the data-sharing agreement while derived statistical parameters, calibration evidence, and model weights remain publishable and openly releasable by the fellow and the host. The distinction between the raw proprietary agronomic data (protected under the data-sharing terms) and the derived scientific outputs (published and released openly) is a practical and legally robust boundary that both protects the associated partner's legitimate proprietary interests and preserves the project's open-science commitments. No further IP complications are anticipated from the use of Sentinel-1 (SAR), Sentinel-2 (optical), ERA5, and PlanetScope data, which are accessed under their respective open-data and commercial-API terms and do not generate proprietary interests in the project's outputs.

Should the demonstrator yield a commercially exploitable feature or a patentable methodology during the fellowship — a possibility that is not excluded but is not anticipated at TRL 3-4 — the fellow and Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest will consult ELTE's technology transfer office to assess whether protection measures are warranted prior to public release. This provision ensures that the project remains responsive to unexpected exploitability signals without prejudging outcomes at the proposal stage in a manner that would be inconsistent with the research-prototype framing.

Proportionality of measures to the scale of the project, and post-project sustainability

The measures described in this dissemination, exploitation, and communication plan are deliberately calibrated to the scale of a 24-month single-researcher European Fellowship producing outputs at TRL 3-4. The plan makes no claim of immediate commercial impact or operational deployment beyond what the demonstrator's TRL 3-4 classification warrants. It does not assert specific publication counts or impact factors, because OBJ-5 (Advancement of the fellow's competences and career) explicitly provides that specific quantitative targets are to be fixed in the Career Development Plan (D4-01, due month 3) with the supervisor Dr. András Jung, reflecting the principle that concrete commitments arise from the actual supervision relationship. The plan is, however, concrete in specifying the mechanisms, the responsible parties, and the timing of each activity:

Within the project (months 1–24): D5-01 (Data management plan) is submitted by month 6, establishing the governance framework for all subsequent open-science activities. Conference presentations are made throughout the second year of the fellowship, with activities documented in D5-02. The demonstrator (OUT-4) is operational and demonstrated to AgroVIR and Hungarian tomato farmers by month 20, as documented in D2-01. Knowledge-exchange events at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest occur at the rate of at least one per project year throughout the fellowship. Open-access publications and FAIR data releases are submitted by month 20 and published by month 24. D5-02 is submitted at month 24, providing the complete audit trail.

After the project (post month 24): The open methodology and codebase release provides a durable scientific contribution to the ERA's geoinformatics and precision-agriculture research community, accessible independently of the fellowship's continuation. The demonstrator (OUT-4) and its validated field evidence (D3-01) serve as a documented proof-of-concept for follow-on funding bids by the fellow and AgroVIR. Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest retains the embedded expertise and training infrastructure developed through the two-way knowledge transfer (WP4), equipping the host to supervise follow-on research and compete for agri-EO grants using the validated methodology. These three post-project sustainability mechanisms — open artefact archive, demonstrator-as-proof-of-concept, and host-embedded expertise — are grounded in the specific deliverables and partner roles of the project rather than in generic aspirational language.

Alignment with the call's expected outcomes and impacts

The dissemination, exploitation, and communication plan, as described, directly addresses the following expected outcomes from the MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026 call:

EO-03 (Enhanced networking and communication capacities with scientific peers, as well as with the general public): addressed through the combination of international conference presentations (scientific peers), open-access publication and FAIR data release (scientific community), research demonstrator showcase via AgroVIR (general public / farming sector), and knowledge-exchange events at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest (academic community).

EO-06 (Increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation of the participating organisation(s)): addressed through the open-access publications and FAIR data releases that carry the imprimatur of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest as the host institution, and through the international conference presentations that position ELTE's geoinformatics and remote-sensing group as a host for cross-disciplinary probabilistic multi-sensor agri-EO research.

EO-07 (Stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations; better transfer of knowledge): addressed through the knowledge-transfer embedding in the host research group (exploitation activity 3) and the open methodology and codebase release (exploitation activity 1), which together increase Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest's capacity to pursue follow-on agri-environmental EO research and make the project's validated methodology available to the broader ERA research community.

EO-08 (Regular feedback of research results into teaching and education at participating organisations): addressed through the structured knowledge-exchange events at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, governed by WP4 and documented in D5-02, which integrate current project results into the host's academic and teaching environment throughout the 24-month fellowship.

The corresponding call-level expected impact EI-03 (Broadened public engagement with research and innovation, increasing societal awareness and uptake of scientific outputs) is addressed through the research demonstrator showcase (OUT-4, WP2) and the documented AgroVIR farmer engagement in WP3, which together constitute a direct and evidence-based route from the project's probabilistic methodology to the farming-sector audience for whom water-use efficiency (RQ6) is operationally relevant. EI-05 (Increased R&I capacity, output, and knowledge transfer among European research organisations) is addressed by the open artefact release (OUT-5, D5-01) and the knowledge-transfer embedding at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest (WP4, D4-01). EI-06 (Enhanced integration of current research results into higher education and teaching at host organisations) is addressed by the knowledge-exchange events at ELTE documented in D5-02.
